A knowledge graph and context manager for AI coding agents.
Claude, Codex, Gemini, Cursor, Copilot and local models.
Shorter sessions, organized projects, fewer tokens.

Check your usage · Live demo · Walkthrough · Results · Install & test · The theory

Abstract

AI coding assistants are billed for every token they read, and in a long conversation they re-read the whole history on every message. Analyzing 284 real Claude Code transcripts (sessions and sub-agent runs), we found that 71% of the cost was spent re-reading context and 97% came from sessions that grew past 150k tokens. Claude was not doing more work. It was carrying more weight.

Rubi attacks the problem from two sides:

  1. Keep sessions short without losing the thread. It compacts early, saves a handoff before each compaction and restores it right after.
  2. Make the project easy to find your way around, so less reading is needed. It builds a map of the code (imports and centrality via PageRank) and a temporal knowledge graph of decisions, bugs, gotchas and concepts. The graph is written by Claude itself, at the moment it already holds that knowledge in context, and searched with a hybrid of BM25, Personalized PageRank and Reciprocal Rank Fusion, within a token budget. Relevant knowledge is recalled automatically on every request, before Claude starts exploring.

Everything is plain markdown inside the project (.rubi/), opens as an Obsidian graph, and runs locally with zero dependencies. It was built for Claude Code and, because its core is a standard MCP server, it also runs in Codex, Gemini CLI, Cursor, GitHub Copilot, Windsurf, Cline, OpenCode, Continue, Goose and Zed, with hosted or local models (see the table).

Results. Two studies, reported as measured, including what did not work:

Study Result
Early compaction, replayed on 284 real transcripts ≈37% lower total cost (simulation on real context curves)
A/B benchmark, 90 sessions, reading a mature graph −37% steps, −37% context re-read, −17% time; billed cost −6% in short cold-start sessions
Same, projected onto the real cost mix (71% cache reads) ≈26% lower cost (projection, not yet measured)

1. The problem: why long sessions get expensive

1.1 Claude has no memory between messages

A language model does not "remember" a conversation. Every time you send a message, the entire conversation so far is sent again: your requests, Claude's answers, and every file it read and every command it ran. That bundle is the context.

In plain words. Imagine a consultant who, before answering each new question, re-reads the whole meeting transcript from the start. Message 10 is cheap. Message 500 means re-reading 499 pages first.

So the cost of a session is not proportional to the number of messages but to the sum of the context sizes. If the context grows by a roughly constant amount per message, that sum grows with the square of the session length.

1.2 Caching helps, but doesn't fix it

Anthropic's prompt caching stores the beginning of the context so that re-reading it costs about 10% of the normal input price. It is a real discount, and in our data it worked: 99% cache hit rate. But 10% of a million tokens, on every message, for hundreds of messages, is still most of the bill. When the cache expires (for example after a pause), the whole context is written to it again at a higher price.

1.3 What the data showed

Rubi ships a token X-ray that reads Claude Code's local transcripts. On 30 days of real usage:

Finding (284 transcripts, 30 days)
Share of cost that was re-reading context (cache reads) 71%
Share of cost from sessions that grew past 150k tokens 97%
Transcripts that peaked above 400k tokens (the largest reached ~970k) 68
Context loaded before the first message (median) 48k
Tool whose outputs weighed most in the context Bash (15%), then Read (4%)
Times the cache expired mid-session and was rewritten 197

Two conclusions drove the design:

  • Sessions are too long. Claude Code only compacts near the model's limit, and with a 1M-token model that is very late.
  • Claude spends a lot of effort finding its way around. A large share of the context is file reads and searches that rediscover how the project works, every new session.

2. Background: the ideas, in plain words

Rubi combines well-known techniques from information retrieval, graph theory and recent research on memory for language models. Each one below gets a plain-words explanation and a pointer to the original work.

2.1 What a knowledge graph does that notes don't

A graph is just things (nodes) connected by relationships (edges). In Rubi the nodes are files, modules, decisions, bugs, gotchas and concepts, and the edges are "file A imports file B", "this decision is about login.ts", "this bug is related to Checkout", "this decision replaces that one".

In plain words. A folder of notes is like a pile of index cards: you only find a card if you guess the word written on it. A graph is like a city map: from where you are, you can see what's next door. Ask about "finishing a purchase" and a plain search finds nothing, because no note says "purchase". With Rubi, Claude adds the related word checkout to the search (section 2.9), the graph finds the concept Checkout, sees that it is linked to a gotcha called "Coupon applied twice" and to the file cupom.ts, and brings those along. You get the trap you were about to fall into, even though you never typed its name.

That is the difference: search finds what matches your words; a graph also finds what is connected to them. In code, connections are everything: who imports whom, which decision affects which file, which bug came back where.

2.2 Ranking by text: BM25

When you search, something has to decide which results come first. BM25 (Robertson & Zaragoza, 2009) is the classic answer used by search engines: a word counts more if it is rare in the collection and frequent in the document, with diminishing returns so repetition doesn't win. Rubi uses it for the textual part of the search, with accent folding, camelCase splitting (PaymentError → payment, error) and light Portuguese/English stemming.

2.3 Who matters most: PageRank

PageRank (Brin & Page, 1998), the algorithm behind early Google, says a page is important if important pages link to it. Applied to code: a file is central if many files import it, especially central ones. Rubi computes PageRank over the import graph to tell Claude, in one line, which files are the backbone of the project. This is the same idea as Aider's repo map.

2.4 Spreading from what matched: Personalized PageRank

Personalized PageRank (Haveliwala, 2002) is PageRank that "starts" from a few chosen nodes and spreads outward, so you get what is important relative to your question. HippoRAG (Gutiérrez et al., 2024) showed this works remarkably well as long-term memory for language models, inspired by how the hippocampus links memories. Rubi seeds it with the nodes that matched your words and lets relevance flow through the graph, discounting "hub" files that everything touches.

2.5 Combining rankings: Reciprocal Rank Fusion

Text, exact file and function names, and graph proximity each produce their own ranked list. Reciprocal Rank Fusion (Cormack et al., 2009) merges them with a simple rule: each list gives every item 1 / (60 + position), and the scores are added. It is robust, needs no tuning, and is what ai-memory also uses.

2.6 Zoom levels: hierarchical summaries

Microsoft's GraphRAG (Edge et al., 2024) showed the value of summarizing a knowledge graph at several levels. Rubi keeps three:

Level File Size When it's read
0 mapa.md ~500 tokens at the start of every session
1 modulos/<module>.md a page per module on demand, with rubi_mapa(module)
2 conhecimento/*.md one file per node found by search

In plain words. Instead of handing someone the whole encyclopedia, you hand them the table of contents and let them open the chapter they need.

2.7 Facts that change: a temporal graph

Decisions change. Zep / Graphiti (Rasmussen et al., 2025) proposed a temporal knowledge graph for agent memory, where facts are invalidated instead of deleted. Rubi does the same: when a new decision replaces an old one, the old node is marked superseded and points to its successor. Claude never follows a stale rule, yet it can still see why things changed. Each node also records the files and the git commit it came from. If a file changed after the note was written, search flags it with ⚠ so Claude double-checks.

2.8 Memory tiers

MemGPT (Packer et al., 2023) framed LLM memory like an operating system: a small core always in context, a working set, and archival storage. Rubi maps that onto core (the level-0 map), working (the current handoff) and archival (the graph, queried on demand).

2.9 The key idea: Claude is the indexer and the semantic search

Most memory systems call another model to extract facts and compute embeddings. Rubi doesn't need one, because Claude is already running:

  • Extraction happens when knowledge is already paid for. At handoff time, or at the end of an answer that required exploring the code, Claude has everything in context. Writing down 3 facts costs a few hundred output tokens. Asking another model later would mean re-reading everything.
  • Semantic search is done by Claude, not by vectors. When Claude queries Rubi it sends termos: synonyms, related concepts and likely function names it imagines. That is the query expansion idea behind HyDE (Gao et al., 2022) and Query2doc (Wang et al., 2023). The LLM supplies the meaning; BM25 and the graph supply the speed.
  • Heavy research runs in a separate window. The bundled rubi-pesquisador subagent explores in its own context and returns only the conclusion, so the main session stays light.
Work Who does it Token cost
Map the code (files, imports, symbols, PageRank) Rubi, deterministic none
Link notes to files and git history Rubi, deterministic none
Extract decisions, bugs, gotchas, concepts Claude, at handoff or at the end of an exploration a few hundred output tokens
Recall what matters for each new request Rubi hook (BM25 + graph over your prompt) none to compute; ≤700 tokens injected, only when something matches
Understand the question (synonyms, related terms) Claude, when calling the search dozens of tokens
Deep exploration of the code rubi-pesquisador subagent isolated from the main context

3. Design: how Rubi works

3.1 What lives in your project

your-project/
├── .rubi/                         ← commit it: your team shares the memory
│   ├── mapa.md                    level 0 · injected at the start of every session
│   ├── modulos/src-checkout.md    level 1 · one per module
│   ├── conhecimento/              level 2 · one markdown file per graph node
│   │   ├── decisao-usar-jwt-em-vez-de-sessao.md
│   │   ├── armadilha-cupom-aplicado-duas-vezes.md
│   │   └── conceito-checkout.md
│   ├── handoffs/2026-10-17-1530.md
│   ├── sessoes/…                  automatic pre-compaction records (git-ignored)
│   └── .indice.json               derived index, rebuildable (git-ignored)
└── CLAUDE.md                      can now be short: it points to the map

A node is ordinary markdown with its type and edges in the frontmatter:

tipo: "decisao"
status: "ativo"

Stateless, so it runs on edge runtimes without a session store.

Personal preferences that apply to every project live in a separate personal vault (~/rubi-vault/_pessoal). Search covers both.

Every item says why it is there ("ligado a…" = linked to, "citado" = named in the question), so Claude can trust or discard it quickly.

4. Results

We ran two studies: a retrospective analysis of real usage, and a controlled A/B benchmark.

4.1 Study 1: early compaction on real sessions

Method. The X-ray reads every Claude Code transcript from the last 30 days (284 transcripts: main sessions and sub-agent runs) and replays each one's actual context curve under a policy that compacts whenever the context passes a threshold and resumes from the fixed context plus an 8k-token handoff. The cost of each compaction (rewriting the new cache prefix) is charged. Costs are in input-token equivalents using Anthropic's price ratios (cache read 0.1×, cache write 1.25–2×, output 5×).

Compaction threshold Window switches Estimated saving on total cost
100k 1,827 ~29%
150k 695 ~37%
250k 336 ~31%

150k was the sweet spot: lower thresholds pay for too many compactions, higher ones carry too much context. This is why Rubi's default is 150k. The interactive demo lets you replay a single session with your own numbers.

4.2 Study 2: controlled A/B benchmark with the knowledge graph

Method. Two public repositories were cloned fresh for every run: Flask (Python) and Hono (TypeScript). For each one we wrote three chained questions about the same area of the code, like three days of work on one feature (see bench/tarefas.json). Each question ran in a new session, so nothing carried over except what was stored on disk.

We separated the two things a memory system does, reading and writing, into four arms:

Arm What runs Question it answers
A Claude Code, no plugin baseline
B Rubi complete, harvesting after every answer that explored ≥4 files what does writing the memory cost?
C Rubi, map + automatic recall, no harvest, empty graph what does reading cost or save with no knowledge yet?
D Same as C, but starting with a graph of 5–6 nodes written by Claude in arm B what does a mature project memory save?
  • Model claude-sonnet-5, read-only tools, 3 repetitions per arm, fresh clone per repetition, 90 sessions in total (round 1: A vs B; round 2: A vs C vs D, re-running A so both rounds have their own baseline).
  • Metrics: the cost Claude Code itself reports (total_cost_usd), turns (API calls), tokens by type, and wall-clock time.
  • A pilot round was discarded: a quoting bug in the benchmark script meant the plugin never loaded in arm B. The script now refuses to record a Rubi arm if the plugin did not run.

4.3 Discussion

Reading a project memory makes Claude much more direct. With a mature graph, Claude needed 37% fewer steps, re-read 37% less context and finished 17% faster. It went straight to the files the memory pointed at instead of searching around. Even with an empty graph, the map and the recall alone cut 21% of the steps.

In this benchmark that only became a 6% lower bill, and here is why. Every question ran in a brand-new, cold session: a single question, then the session ends. In that setting the most expensive part is writing the cache from scratch (cache writes cost 2× the input price), and that part is the same with or without Rubi. The savings land on cache reads and output, which are a small share of a 3-to-5-turn session.

Real work looks the other way around. In the 284 real transcripts of Study 1, cache reads were 71% of the cost, writes ~20% and output ~10%. Applying arm D's measured changes to that real mix (reads −37%, writes +8%, output −26%) gives:

0.71 × 0.63  +  0.20 × 1.08  +  0.10 × 0.74  =  0.737   →  ≈ 26% lower cost

That is a projection, not a measurement. Measuring it properly needs long, multi-task sessions on a real project; that is the next benchmark.

Answer quality. A spot check found the answers equivalent, with one telling difference. On the Flask teardown question, the baseline answer cited RequestContext.pop, a class that no longer exists in current Flask (it was merged into AppContext), most likely recalled from training data. The answer with a mature graph got it right, because the graph held the fact "AppContext and RequestContext were unified", written by Claude after reading the actual code. A memory of this codebase beats the model's memory of old versions of it. That is one observation, not a measured rate.

Writing on every answer does not pay in short sessions. Arm B's harvest (an extra tool load plus an extra call that re-reads the context) cost 15% more, and three short sessions are not enough to earn it back. Following this result, Rubi's default changed: the harvest now only triggers after heavy exploration (≥10 reads/searches with nothing saved), and the main extraction happens at the meter (80% of the window), when the context is already large and paid for.

Where the money is today. Of everything measured, the largest lever is still keeping sessions short (Study 1: about 37% of total cost, simulated on real usage). The knowledge graph's measured contribution is fewer steps and less re-reading, which compounds in long sessions and on codebases the model has never seen. Flask and Hono are famous projects the model partly knows from training, the least favorable case for a memory.

5. Walkthrough: a week with Rubi

Monday, install (2 minutes).

/plugin marketplace add YURIBEDRAN/rubi
/plugin install rubi@rubi

Then node scripts/instalar.mjs from a clone of this repo turns on early compaction (150k) and creates your personal vault. Details in Install.

Monday, first session. You open Claude Code in your project. Rubi indexes the code in under a second for most projects and injects the map:

[rubi] Mapa do projeto (nível 0)
## Módulos
- src/checkout (8) — centrais: Checkout.tsx, useCart.ts, api.ts
- src/desconto (4) — centrais: cupom.ts, regras.ts
## Arquivos centrais
`src/lib/api.ts` · `src/types.ts` · `src/checkout/Checkout.tsx` …

Claude already knows where things live before you ask anything.

Monday, you ask: "why is the coupon applied twice?" Claude calls rubi_contexto with related terms (discount, cart, aplicarCupom), goes straight to cupom.ts, finds the bug and fixes it. When it finishes, the harvest hook asks it to save what it learned:

rubi_registrar → criado: conhecimento/bug-cupom-aplicado-duas-vezes.md
                 criado: conhecimento/conceito-checkout.md

Tuesday, new session, related task: "add a second coupon type." Before Claude reads anything, Rubi's recall hook searches the graph with your request and injects the bug note, the concept Checkout and the files involved. Claude doesn't rediscover the checkout flow. It reads two files instead of ten.

Wednesday, a long refactor. The context grows. At 120k the meter tells Claude to register the decisions it made and save a handoff. At 150k Claude Code compacts on its own. Rubi saves a record of the session and, right after compaction, injects the handoff back. You keep talking; Claude keeps going from ~60k instead of dragging 500k along.

Thursday, a decision changes. "Let's use JWT instead of session cookies." Claude registers the new decision with substitui: "Sessão em cookie". The old one is marked superseded, never deleted, and no future session will follow it.

Friday, look at it. Open .rubi/ in Obsidian and switch to graph view: modules, decisions, bugs and concepts, connected. Run /rubi:raio-x to see where the week's tokens went, and /rubi:organizar if your CLAUDE.md has grown fat. It moves the details into the graph and leaves only the rules that matter in every message.

6. Limitations and threats to validity

  • Small benchmark. Two repositories, three chained tasks, 3 repetitions per arm (90 sessions). LLM runs vary between executions (standard deviation up to $0.05 per 3-session run on Flask); treat the numbers as indicative. The benchmark is in the repo so it can be rerun and extended.
  • Cold, short sessions. Each benchmark question is a one-shot session, which favors cache writes over cache reads and hides most of the reading savings. The 26% figure for real usage is a projection.
  • The seed graph for arm D came from arm B's own runs on the same questions, so it is relevant by construction. A real project memory is built from many different tasks, so it is broader and noisier.
  • Famous repositories. Flask and Hono are well known, so the model already knows parts of them from training, which favors the baseline. Private, less-known codebases should benefit more from a map and a graph. We have not measured that yet.
  • The graph is only as good as what is registered. Claude decides what to store. The harvest hook and the meter make it happen at the right moments, but extraction quality depends on the model.
  • Overhead on tiny tasks. The map (~500 tokens) and the tool definitions are a fixed cost. On a one-shot question that needs no exploration, Rubi can cost slightly more than nothing.
  • Code map is regex-based, not a full parser (no tree-sitter, to keep zero dependencies). Imports are resolved for JS/TS (relative and @/ aliases), Python, Go, Rust, Java/Kotlin, PHP, Ruby, C/C++, CSS and Dart. Dynamic imports and exotic aliases may be missed.
  • No vector embeddings. Meaning comes from Claude's own query expansion. For very large knowledge bases (tens of thousands of nodes), an embedding index could be added later; the JSON index can also be swapped for SQLite FTS5.
  • Hooks cannot run /clear or /compact, nor edit Claude Code's compaction summary. Rubi works around it: Claude Code compacts at the threshold you set, and Rubi handles what happens before and after.
  • Platforms. The benchmark was run on Claude Code only. Claude Code and Codex were tested end to end; the other agents are configured from their official docs and not yet tested end to end. Agents without context-injecting hooks rely on the model following instructions. The Claude website and mobile app are not supported yet.

7. Install

You need Node 18+ (node --version to check; get it at nodejs.org).

Claude Code, step by step

1. Install the plugin. Open Claude Code in any project and type:

/plugin marketplace add YURIBEDRAN/rubi
/plugin install rubi@rubi

Restart Claude Code (exit and run claude again) so the hooks load.

2. Turn on early compaction (recommended). In a terminal:

git clone https://github.com/YURIBEDRAN/rubi
cd rubi
node scripts/instalar.mjs

It asks two things: where to keep your personal notes (default ~/rubi-vault) and when to compact (default 150000 tokens). It writes CLAUDE_CODE_AUTO_COMPACT_WINDOW into ~/.claude/settings.json, keeping a backup in settings.json.bak-rubi. Undo any time with node scripts/instalar.mjs --desfazer.

3. Check that it works. Open Claude Code inside a project that uses git.

Try this You should see
Start a session A .rubi/ folder appears in the project, with mapa.md listing your modules and central files
Ask: "what do you know about this project's structure?" Claude answers using the map (modules, central files) without exploring first
Ask: "use Rubi to register a decision: we use Postgres because the client already runs it" criado: conhecimento/decisao-...md, and the file appears in .rubi/conhecimento/
Exit, start a new session and ask "why did we choose Postgres?" Claude answers from memory: the recall hook injected the decision
Type /rubi:raio-x A breakdown of where your tokens went in the last 30 days

Note

.rubi/ is meant to be committed so your team shares the memory. Its own .gitignore already leaves out the derived index and the automatic session records. If you'd rather keep it private, add .rubi/ to your project's .gitignore.

To try Rubi without installing it: claude --plugin-dir path/to/rubi.

Claude Desktop, step by step

1. Download rubi.mcpb from Releases.

2. Double-click the file, or drag it into Claude Desktop under Settings → Extensions, and click Install.

3. Optionally choose a vault folder. Pick an empty folder used only by Rubi (for example Documents/Rubi) or an Obsidian vault. Leave it blank to use ~/rubi-vault. Don't point it at a busy folder like Downloads.

4. Make sure the extension is turned on in Settings → Extensions.

5. Check that it works.

Try this You should see
"Use Rubi to register a preference: I like practical examples" Claude confirms it was registered, and a file appears in <vault>/_pessoal/conhecimento/
In a new conversation: "look up my preferences in Rubi" Claude finds "I like practical examples"

If Claude says it can't find a tool called Rubi, the extension is turned off: switch it on in Settings → Extensions and start a new conversation.

In the Desktop app, Rubi provides the memory: the knowledge graph, hybrid search and handoffs. The code map and the automatic hooks (recall, meter, harvest, early compaction) need Claude Code. Claude Desktop also has its own built-in memory, so mention Rubi when you want something stored there.

Codex, Gemini CLI, Cursor, Copilot and other agents

Rubi's core is a standard MCP server, so it works in any coding agent that speaks MCP, with the vendor's models or with local models. One command connects it:

git clone https://github.com/YURIBEDRAN/rubi

The problem: why long sessions get expensive 1.1 Claude has no memory between messages A language model does not "remember" a conversation. Every time you send a message, the entire conversation so far is sent again: your requests, Claude's answers, and every file it read and every command it ran. That bundle is the context. In plain words. Imagine a consultant who, before answering each new question, re-reads the whole meeting transcript from the start. Message 10 is cheap. Message 500 means re-reading 499 pages first. So the cost of a session is not proportional to the number of messages but to the sum of the context sizes. If the context grows by a roughly constant amount per message, that sum grows with the square of the session length. 1.2 Caching helps, but doesn't fix it Anthropic's prompt caching stores the beginning of the context so that re-reading it costs about 10% of the normal input price. It is a real discount, and in our data it worked: 99% cache hit rate. But 10% of a million tokens, on every message, for hundreds of messages, is still most of the bill. When the cache expires (for example after a pause), the whole context is written to it again at a higher price. 1.3 What the data showed Rubi ships a token X-ray that reads Claude Code's local transcripts. On 30 days of real usage: Finding (284 transcripts, 30 days) Share of cost that was re-reading context (cache reads) 71% Share of cost from sessions that grew past 150k tokens 97% Transcripts that peaked above 400k tokens (the largest reached ~970k) 68 Context loaded before the first message (median) 48k Tool whose outputs weighed most in the context Bash (15%), then Read (4%) Times the cache expired mid-session and was rewritten 197 Two conclusions drove the design: Sessions are too long. Claude Code only compacts near the model's limit, and with a 1M-token model that is very late. Claude spends a lot of effort finding its way around. A large share of the context is file reads and searches that rediscover how the project works, every new session. 2. Background: the ideas, in plain words Rubi combines well-known techniques from information retrieval, graph theory and recent research on memory for language models. Each one below gets a plain-words explanation and a pointer to the original work. 2.1 What a knowledge graph does that notes don't A graph is just things (nodes) connected by relationships (edges). In Rubi the nodes are files, modules, decisions, bugs, gotchas and concepts, and the edges are "file A imports file B", "this decision is about login.ts", "this bug is related to Checkout", "this decision replaces that one". In plain words. A folder of notes is like a pile of index cards: you only find a card if you guess the word written on it. A graph is like a city map: from where you are, you can see what's next door. Ask about "finishing a purchase" and a plain search finds nothing, because no note says "purchase". With Rubi, Claude adds the related word checkout to the search (section 2.9), the graph finds the concept Checkout, sees that it is linked to a gotcha called "Coupon applied twice" and to the file cupom.ts, and brings those along. You get the trap you were about to fall into, even though you never typed its name. That is the difference: search finds what matches your words; a graph also finds what is connected to them. In code, connections are everything: who imports whom, which decision affects which file, which bug came back where. 2.2 Ranking by text: BM25 When you search, something has to decide which results come first. BM25 (Robertson & Zaragoza, 2009) is the classic answer used by search engines: a word counts more if it is rare in the collection and frequent in the document, with diminishing returns so repetition doesn't win. Rubi uses it for the textual part of the search, with accent folding, camelCase splitting (PaymentError → payment, error) and light Portuguese/English stemming. 2.3 Who matters most: PageRank PageRank (Brin & Page, 1998), the algorithm behind early Google, says a page is important if important pages link to it. Applied to code: a file is central if many files import it, especially central ones. Rubi computes PageRank over the import graph to tell Claude, in one line, which files are the backbone of the project. This is the same idea as Aider's repo map. 2.4 Spreading from what matched: Personalized PageRank Personalized PageRank (Haveliwala, 2002) is PageRank that "starts" from a few chosen nodes and spreads outward, so you get what is important relative to your question. HippoRAG (Gutiérrez et al., 2024) showed this works remarkably well as long-term memory for language models, inspired by how the hippocampus links memories. Rubi seeds it with the nodes that matched your words and lets relevance flow through the graph, discounting "hub" files that everything touches. 2.5 Combining rankings: Reciprocal Rank Fusion Text, exact file and function names, and graph proximity each produce their own ranked list. Reciprocal Rank Fusion (Cormack et al., 2009) merges them with a simple rule: each list gives every item 1 / (60 + position), and the scores are added. It is robust, needs no tuning, and is what ai-memory also uses. 2.6 Zoom levels: hierarchical summaries Microsoft's GraphRAG (Edge et al., 2024) showed the value of summarizing a knowledge graph at several levels. Rubi keeps three: Level File Size When it's read 0 mapa.md ~500 tokens at the start of every session 1 modulos/<module>.md a page per module on demand, with rubi_mapa(module) 2 conhecimento/*.md one file per node found by search In plain words. Instead of handing someone the whole encyclopedia, you hand them the table of contents and let them open the chapter they need. 2.7 Facts that change: a temporal graph Decisions change. Zep / Graphiti (Rasmussen et al., 2025) proposed a temporal knowledge graph for agent memory, where facts are invalidated instead of deleted. Rubi does the same: when a new decision replaces an old one, the old node is marked superseded and points to its successor. Claude never follows a stale rule, yet it can still see why things changed. Each node also records the files and the git commit it came from. If a file changed after the note was written, search flags it with ⚠ so Claude double-checks. 2.8 Memory tiers MemGPT (Packer et al., 2023) framed LLM memory like an operating system: a small core always in context, a working set, and archival storage. Rubi maps that onto core (the level-0 map), working (the current handoff) and archival (the graph, queried on demand). 2.9 The key idea: Claude is the indexer and the semantic search Most memory systems call another model to extract facts and compute embeddings. Rubi doesn't need one, because Claude is already running: Extraction happens when knowledge is already paid for. At handoff time, or at the end of an answer that required exploring the code, Claude has everything in context. Writing down 3 facts costs a few hundred output tokens. Asking another model later would mean re-reading everything. Semantic search is done by Claude, not by vectors. When Claude queries Rubi it sends termos: synonyms, related concepts and likely function names it imagines. That is the query expansion idea behind HyDE (Gao et al., 2022) and Query2doc (Wang et al., 2023). The LLM supplies the meaning; BM25 and the graph supply the speed. Every question ran in a brand-new, cold session: a single question, then the session ends. In that setting the most expensive part is writing the cache from scratch (cache writes cost 2× the input price), and that part is the same with or without Rubi. Two repositories, three chained tasks, 3 repetitions per arm (90 sessions). LLM runs vary between executions (standard deviation up to $0.05 per 3-session run on Flask); treat the numbers as indicative. The benchmark is in the repo so it can be rerun and extended. Cold, short sessions. Each benchmark question is a one-shot session, which favors cache writes over cache reads and hides most of the reading savings. The 26% figure for real usage is a projection. The seed graph for arm D came from arm B's own runs on the same questions, so it is relevant by construction. A real project memory is built from many different tasks, so it is broader and noisier. Famous repositories. Flask and Hono are well known, so the model already knows parts of them from training, which favors the baseline. Private, less-known codebases should benefit more from a map and a graph. We have not measured that yet. The graph is only as good as what is registered. Claude decides what to store. The harvest hook and the meter make it happen at the right moments, but extraction quality depends on the model. Overhead on tiny tasks. The map (~500 tokens) and the tool definitions are a fixed cost. On a one-shot question that needs no exploration, Rubi can cost slightly more than nothing. Code map is regex-based, not a full parser (no tree-sitter, to keep zero dependencies). Imports are resolved for JS/TS (relative and @/ aliases), Python, Go, Rust, Java/Kotlin, PHP, Ruby, C/C++, CSS and Dart. Dynamic imports and exotic aliases may be missed. No vector embeddings. Meaning comes from Claude's own query expansion. For very large knowledge bases (tens of thousands of nodes), an embedding index could be added later; the JSON index can also be swapped for SQLite FTS5. Hooks cannot run /clear or /compact, nor edit Claude Code's compaction summary. Rubi works around it: Claude Code compacts at the threshold you set, and Rubi handles what happens before and after. Platforms. The benchmark was run on Claude Code only. Claude Code and Codex were tested end to end; the other agents are configured from their official docs and not yet tested end to end. Agents without context-injecting hooks rely on the model following instructions. The Claude website and mobile app are not supported yet. 7. Open Claude Code in any project and type: /plugin marketplace add YURIBEDRAN/rubi /plugin install rubi@rubi Restart Claude Code (exit and run claude again) so the hooks load. 2. Turn on early compaction (recommended). In a terminal: git clone https://github.com/YURIBEDRAN/rubi cd rubi node scripts/instalar.mjs It asks two things: where to keep your personal notes (default ~/rubi-vault) and when to compact (default 150000 tokens). Try this You should see Start a session A .rubi/ folder appears in the project, with mapa.md listing your modules and central files Ask: "what do you know about this project's structure?" Claude answers from memory: the recall hook injected the decision Type /rubi:raio-x A breakdown of where your tokens went in the last 30 days Note.rubi/ is meant to be committed so your team shares the memory. blocks.html_en: A graph is just things (nodes) connected by relationships (edges). In Rubi the nodes are files, modules, decisions, bugs, gotchas and concepts, and the edges are "file A imports file B", "this decision is about login.ts", "this bug is related to Checkout", "this decision replaces that one".

blocks.html_en: In plain words. A folder of notes is like a pile of index cards: you only find a card if you guess the word written on it. A graph is like a city map: from where you are, you can see what's next door. Ask about "finishing a purchase" and a plain search finds nothing, because no note says "purchase". You get the trap you were about to fall into, even though you never typed its name.

blocks.html_en: When you search, something has to decide which results come first. BM25 (Robertson & Zaragoza, 2009) is the classic answer used by search engines: a word counts more if it is rare in the collection and frequent in the document, with diminishing returns so repetition doesn't win. Rubi uses it for the textual part of the search, with accent folding, camelCase splitting (PaymentError → payment, error) and light Portuguese/English stemming.

blocks.html_en: Personalized PageRank (Haveliwala, 2002) is PageRank that "starts" from a few chosen nodes and spreads outward, so you get what is important relative to your question. HippoRAG (Gutiérrez et al., 2024) showed this works remarkably well as long-term memory for language models, inspired by how the hippocampus links memories. Rubi seeds it with the nodes that matched your words and lets relevance flow through the graph, discounting "hub" files that everything touches.

content_html_zh:
A knowledge graph and context manager for AI coding agents.Claude, Codex, Gemini, Cursor, Copilot and local models.Shorter sessions, organized projects, fewer tokens.

Check your usage · Live demo · Walkthrough · Results · Install & test · The theory

抽象的

AI coding assistants are billed for every token they read, and in a long conversation they re-read the whole history on every message. Analyzing 284 real Claude Code transcripts (sessions and sub-agent runs), we found that 71% of the cost was spent re-reading context and 97% came from sessions that grew past 150k tokens. Claude was not doing more work. It was carrying more weight.

Rubi attacks the problem from two sides:

  1. Keep sessions short without losing the thread. It compacts early, saves a handoff before each compaction and restores it right after.
  2. Make the project easy to find your way around, so less reading is needed. It builds a map of the code (imports and centrality via PageRank) and a temporal knowledge graph of decisions, bugs, gotchas and concepts. The graph is written by Claude itself, at the moment it already holds that knowledge in context, and searched with a hybrid of BM25, Personalized PageRank and Reciprocal Rank Fusion, within a token budget. Relevant knowledge is recalled automatically on every request, before Claude starts exploring.

Everything is plain markdown inside the project (.rubi/), opens as an Obsidian graph, and runs locally with zero dependencies. It was built for Claude Code and, because its core is a standard MCP server, it also runs in Codex, Gemini CLI, Cursor, GitHub Copilot, Windsurf, Cline, OpenCode, Continue, Goose and Zed, with hosted or local models (see the table).

结果。 Two studies, reported as measured, including what did not work:

Study 结果
Early compaction, replayed on 284 real transcripts ≈37% lower total cost (simulation on real context curves)
A/B benchmark, 90 sessions, reading a mature graph −37% steps, −37% context re-read, −17% time; billed cost −6% in short cold-start sessions
Same, projected onto the real cost mix (71% cache reads) ≈26% lower cost (projection, not yet measured)
A/B benchmark, writing memory after every answer +15% cost in short sessions, so the default was changed to write less often

1. The problem: why long sessions get expensive

1.1 Claude has no memory between messages

A language model does not "remember" a conversation. Every time you send a message, the entire conversation so far is sent again: your requests, Claude's answers, and every file it read and every command it ran. That bundle is the context.

In plain words. Imagine a consultant who, before answering each new question, re-reads the whole meeting transcript from the start. Message 10 is cheap. Message 500 means re-reading 499 pages first.

So the cost of a session is not proportional to the number of messages but to the sum of the context sizes. If the context grows by a roughly constant amount per message, that sum grows with the square of the session length.

1.2 Caching helps, but doesn't fix it

Anthropic's prompt caching stores the beginning of the context so that re-reading it costs about 10% of the normal input price. It is a real discount, and in our data it worked: 99% cache hit rate. But 10% of a million tokens, on every message, for hundreds of messages, is still most of the bill. When the cache expires (for example after a pause), the whole context is written to it again at a higher price.

1.3 What the data showed

Rubi ships a token X-ray that reads Claude Code's local transcripts. On 30 days of real usage:

Finding (284 transcripts, 30 days)
Share of cost that was re-reading context (cache reads) 71%
Share of cost from sessions that grew past 150k tokens 97%
Transcripts that peaked above 400k tokens (the largest reached ~970k) 68
Context loaded before the first message (median) 48k
Tool whose outputs weighed most in the context Bash (15%), then Read (4%)
Times the cache expired mid-session and was rewritten 197

Two conclusions drove the design:

  • Sessions are too long. Claude Code only compacts near the model's limit, and with a 1M-token model that is very late.
  • Claude spends a lot of effort finding its way around. A large share of the context is file reads and searches that rediscover how the project works, every new session.

2. Background: the ideas, in plain words

Rubi combines well-known techniques from information retrieval, graph theory and recent research on memory for language models. Each one below gets a plain-words explanation and a pointer to the original work.

2.1 What a knowledge graph does that notes don't

A graph is just things (nodes) connected by relationships (edges). In Rubi the nodes are files, modules, decisions, bugs, gotchas and concepts, and the edges are "file A imports file B", "this decision is about login.ts", "this bug is related to Checkout", "this decision replaces that one".

In plain words. A folder of notes is like a pile of index cards: you only find a card if you guess the word written on it. A graph is like a city map: from where you are, you can see what's next door. Ask about "finishing a purchase" and a plain search finds nothing, because no note says "purchase". With Rubi, Claude adds the related word checkout to the search (section 2.9), the graph finds the concept Checkout, sees that it is linked to a gotcha called "Coupon applied twice" and to the file cupom.ts, and brings those along. You get the trap you were about to fall into, even though you never typed its name.

That is the difference: search finds what matches your words; a graph also finds what is connected to them. In code, connections are everything: who imports whom, which decision affects which file, which bug came back where.

2.2 Ranking by text: BM25

When you search, something has to decide which results come first. BM25 (Robertson & Zaragoza, 2009) is the classic answer used by search engines: a word counts more if it is rare in the collection and frequent in the document, with diminishing returns so repetition doesn't win. Rubi uses it for the textual part of the search, with accent folding, camelCase splitting (PaymentError → payment, error) and light Portuguese/English stemming.

2.3 Who matters most: PageRank

PageRank (Brin & Page, 1998), the algorithm behind early Google, says a page is important if important pages link to it. Applied to code: a file is central if many files import it, especially central ones. Rubi computes PageRank over the import graph to tell Claude, in one line, which files are the backbone of the project. This is the same idea as Aider's repo map.

2.4 Spreading from what matched: Personalized PageRank

Personalized PageRank (Haveliwala, 2002) is PageRank that "starts" from a few chosen nodes and spreads outward, so you get what is important relative to your question. HippoRAG (Gutiérrez et al., 2024) showed this works remarkably well as long-term memory for language models, inspired by how the hippocampus links memories. Rubi seeds it with the nodes that matched your words and lets relevance flow through the graph, discounting "hub" files that everything touches.

2.5 Combining rankings: Reciprocal Rank Fusion

Text, exact file and function names, and graph proximity each produce their own ranked list. Reciprocal Rank Fusion (Cormack et al., 2009) merges them with a simple rule: each list gives every item 1 / (60 + position), and the scores are added. It is robust, needs no tuning, and is what ai-memory also uses.

2.6 Zoom levels: hierarchical summaries

Microsoft's GraphRAG (Edge et al., 2024) showed the value of summarizing a knowledge graph at several levels. Rubi keeps three:

Level File Size When it's read
0 mapa.md ~500 tokens at the start of every session
1 modulos/<module>.md a page per module on demand, with rubi_mapa(module)
2 conhecimento/*.md one file per node found by search
In plain words. Instead of handing someone the whole encyclopedia, you hand them the table of contents and let them open the chapter they need.

2.7 Facts that change: a temporal graph

Decisions change. Zep / Graphiti (Rasmussen et al., 2025) proposed a temporal knowledge graph for agent memory, where facts are invalidated instead of deleted. Rubi does the same: when a new decision replaces an old one, the old node is marked superseded and points to its successor. Claude never follows a stale rule, yet it can still see why things changed. Each node also records the files and the git commit it came from. If a file changed after the note was written, search flags it with ⚠ so Claude double-checks.

2.8 Memory tiers

MemGPT (Packer et al., 2023) framed LLM memory like an operating system: a small core always in context, a working set, and archival storage. Rubi maps that onto core (the level-0 map), working (the current handoff) and archival (the graph, queried on demand).

2.9 The key idea: Claude is the indexer and the semantic search

Most memory systems call another model to extract facts and compute embeddings. Rubi doesn't need one, because Claude is already running:

  • Extraction happens when knowledge is already paid for. At handoff time, or at the end of an answer that required exploring the code, Claude has everything in context. Writing down 3 facts costs a few hundred output tokens. Asking another model later would mean re-reading everything.
  • Semantic search is done by Claude, not by vectors. When Claude queries Rubi it sends termos: synonyms, related concepts and likely function names it imagines. That is the query expansion idea behind HyDE (Gao et al., 2022) and Query2doc (Wang et al., 2023). The LLM supplies the meaning; BM25 and the graph supply the speed.
  • Heavy research runs in a separate window. The bundled rubi-pesquisador subagent explores in its own context and returns only the conclusion, so the main session stays light.

3.1 What lives in your project

4. 结果

We ran two studies: a retrospective analysis of real usage, and a controlled A/B benchmark.

4.1 Study 1: early compaction on real sessions

Method. The X-ray reads every Claude Code transcript from the last 30 days (284 transcripts: main sessions and sub-agent runs) and replays each one's actual context curve under a policy that compacts whenever the context passes a threshold and resumes from the fixed context plus an 8k-token handoff. The cost of each compaction (rewriting the new cache prefix) is charged. Costs are in input-token equivalents using Anthropic's price ratios (cache read 0.1×, cache write 1.25–2×, output 5×).

Compaction threshold Window switches Estimated saving on total cost
100k 1,827 ~29%
150k 695 ~37%
250k 336 ~31%

150k was the sweet spot: lower thresholds pay for too many compactions, higher ones carry too much context. This is why Rubi's default is 150k. The interactive demo lets you replay a single session with your own numbers.

4.2 Study 2: controlled A/B benchmark with the knowledge graph

Method. Two public repositories were cloned fresh for every run: Flask (Python) and Hono (TypeScript). For each one we wrote three chained questions about the same area of the code, like three days of work on one feature (see bench/tarefas.json). Each question ran in a new session, so nothing carried over except what was stored on disk.

We separated the two things a memory system does, reading and writing, into four arms:

  • Model claude-sonnet-5, read-only tools, 3 repetitions per arm, fresh clone per repetition, 90 sessions in total (round 1: A vs B; round 2: A vs C vs D, re-running A so both rounds have their own baseline).

4.3 Discussion

Reading a project memory makes Claude much more direct. With a mature graph, Claude needed 37% fewer steps, re-read 37% less context and finished 17% faster. It went straight to the files the memory pointed at instead of searching around. Even with an empty graph, the map and the recall alone cut 21% of the steps.

In this benchmark that only became a 6% lower bill, and here is why. Every question ran in a brand-new, cold session: a single question, then the session ends. In that setting the most expensive part is writing the cache from scratch (cache writes cost 2× the input price), and that part is the same with or without Rubi. The savings land on cache reads and output, which are a small share of a 3-to-5-turn session.

Real work looks the other way around. In the 284 real transcripts of Study 1, cache reads were 71% of the cost, writes ~20% and output ~10%. Applying arm D's measured changes to that real mix (reads −37%, writes +8%, output −26%) gives:

0.71 × 0.63  +  0.20 × 1.08  +  0.10 × 0.74  =  0.737   →  ≈ 26% lower cost

That is a projection, not a measurement. Measuring it properly needs long, multi-task sessions on a real project; that is the next benchmark.

Answer quality. A spot check found the answers equivalent, with one telling difference. On the Flask teardown question, the baseline answer cited RequestContext.pop, a class that no longer exists in current Flask (it was merged into AppContext), most likely recalled from training data. The answer with a mature graph got it right, because the graph held the fact "AppContext and RequestContext were unified", written by Claude after reading the actual code. A memory of this codebase beats the model's memory of old versions of it. That is one observation, not a measured rate.

Writing on every answer does not pay in short sessions. Arm B's harvest (an extra tool load plus an extra call that re-reads the context) cost 15% more, and three short sessions are not enough to earn it back. Following this result, Rubi's default changed: the harvest now only triggers after heavy exploration (≥10 reads/searches with nothing saved), and the main extraction happens at the meter (80% of the window), when the context is already large and paid for.

Where the money is today. Of everything measured, the largest lever is still keeping sessions short (Study 1: about 37% of total cost, simulated on real usage). The knowledge graph's measured contribution is fewer steps and less re-reading, which compounds in long sessions and on codebases the model has never seen. Flask and Hono are famous projects the model partly knows from training, the least favorable case for a memory.

6. Limitations and threats to validity

  • Small benchmark. Two repositories, three chained tasks, 3 repetitions per arm (90 sessions). LLM runs vary between executions (standard deviation up to $0.05 per 3-session run on Flask); treat the numbers as indicative. The benchmark is in the repo so it can be rerun and extended.
  • Cold, short sessions. Each benchmark question is a one-shot session, which favors cache writes over cache reads and hides most of the reading savings. The 26% figure for real usage is a projection.
  • The seed graph for arm D came from arm B's own runs on the same questions, so it is relevant by construction. A real project memory is built from many different tasks, so it is broader and noisier.
  • Famous repositories. Flask and Hono are well known, so the model already knows parts of them from training, which favors the baseline. Private, less-known codebases should benefit more from a map and a graph. We have not measured that yet.
  • The graph is only as good as what is registered. Claude decides what to store. The harvest hook and the meter make it happen at the right moments, but extraction quality depends on the model.
  • Overhead on tiny tasks. The map (~500 tokens) and the tool definitions are a fixed cost. On a one-shot question that needs no exploration, Rubi can cost slightly more than nothing.
  • Code map is regex-based, not a full parser (no tree-sitter, to keep zero dependencies). Imports are resolved for JS/TS (relative and @/ aliases), Python, Go, Rust, Java/Kotlin, PHP, Ruby, C/C++, CSS and Dart. Dynamic imports and exotic aliases may be missed.
  • No vector embeddings. Meaning comes from Claude's own query expansion. For very large knowledge bases (tens of thousands of nodes), an embedding index could be added later; the JSON index can also be swapped for SQLite FTS5.
  • Hooks cannot run /clear or /compact, nor edit Claude Code's compaction summary. Rubi works around it: Claude Code compacts at the threshold you set, and Rubi handles what happens before and after.
  • 平台。 The benchmark was run on Claude Code only. Claude Code and Codex were tested end to end; the other agents are configured from their official docs and not yet tested end to end. Agents without context-injecting hooks rely on the model following instructions. The Claude website and mobile app are not supported yet.

7. 安装

You need Node 18+ (node --version to check; get it at nodejs.org).

Claude Code, step by step

1. Install the plugin. Open Claude Code in any project and type:

/plugin marketplace add YURIBEDRAN/rubi
/plugin install rubi@rubi

Restart Claude Code (exit and run claude again) so the hooks load.

2. Turn on early compaction (recommended). In a terminal:

git clone https://github.com/YURIBEDRAN/rubi
cd rubi
node scripts/instalar.mjs

It asks two things: where to keep your personal notes (default ~/rubi-vault) and when to compact (default 150000 tokens). It writes CLAUDE_CODE_AUTO_COMPACT_WINDOW into ~/.claude/settings.json, keeping a backup in settings.json.bak-rubi. Undo any time with node scripts/instalar.mjs --desfazer.

3. Check that it works. Open Claude Code inside a project that uses git.

.rubi/ is meant to be committed so your team shares the memory. Its own .gitignore already leaves out the derived index and the automatic session records. If you'd rather keep it private, add .rubi/ to your project's .gitignore.

To try Rubi without installing it: claude --plugin-dir path/to/rubi.

2. Double-click the file, or drag it into Claude Desktop under Settings → Extensions, and click Install.

Codex, Gemini CLI, Cursor, Copilot and other agents

Rubi's core is a standard MCP server, so it works in any coding agent that speaks MCP, with the vendor's models or with local models. One command connects it:

git clone https://github.com/YURIBEDRAN/rubi
cd your-project
node /path/to/rubi/scripts/conectar.mjs codex     # or: gemini, cursor, vscode, windsurf, cline, opencode, continue, goose, zed

For each agent it registers the MCP server in that agent's config (keeping a .bak-rubi backup), writes the instructions into the file the agent reads on its own (AGENTS.md, GEMINI.md, .cursor/rules/rubi.mdc...) and, where the agent supports hooks that feed context to the model, turns on the map at session start and the automatic recall on every request. Formats that are risky to edit automatically (YAML, JSON with comments) are printed for you to paste. Use --so-mostrar to only print, never write. --listar shows all agents.

Codex asks you to approve new hooks once: open Codex and type /hooks to review and trust Rubi's two hooks.
